items.stem: Grasshopper in grassland is a

options.label: A
options.text: producer

options.label: B
options.text: herbivore

options.label: C
options.text: carnivore

options.label: D
options.text: none of the above

items.answer: The plant is the producer and the animals are consumers. The first consumer in the chain is called the primary consumer, the next one the secondary consumer and the one after that the tertiary consumer. A consumer that eats plants is called a herbivore (grasshopper), and a consumer that eats other animals is called a carnivore (frog and hawk). An omnivore is an animal that eats both plants and animals. Thus (b) is the correct option.

items.answer: Vultures are scavenging birds that feed on dead animals. Vultures do not kill their own prey, they feed on dead animals. items.stem: What must be preserved in an ecosystem, if the system needs to be maintained?

options.label: A
options.text: Producers and carnivores

options.label: B
options.text: Producers and decomposers

options.label: C
options.text: Carnivores and decomposers

options.label: D
options.text: Herbivores and carnivores

items.answer: The most important characteristics of any ecosystem are energy flow and cycling of materials. Producers and decomposers are indispensable for any ecosystem. Producers trap solar energy and convert it into a usable form as carbohydrates, which are passed on to successive levels through food chains and food webs. The other important characteristic of the ecosystem is the cycling of materials, called the bio-geochemical cycles, in which decomposers are the most important because they release the mineral nutrients back to the environment. Thus (b) is the correct option.

items.stem: Describe with the help of diagram how energy flows through different trophic levels in a food chain.
items.answer: The energy moves progressively through various trophic levels of a food chain in the form of food. Green plants are producers which capture about 2-4% of the energy of sunlight and convert it into food energy. When green plants are eaten by primary consumers, a great deal of energy is lost as heat to the environment. According to Lindeman's ten percent law, only 10% of the energy entering a particular trophic level of a food chain is available for transfer to the next higher trophic level. This means that the energy available at each successive trophic level is 10% of the previous level. For example, Grass → Deer → Lion. As little energy is available for the next level of consumers, food chains generally consist of only three or four steps. Flow of energy is unidirectional as the energy captured by the autotrophs does not revert back to the solar input and the energy which passes to the herbivores does not come back to autotrophs. items.stem: What is the 10 percent law? Explain with an example.
items.answer:
During the transfer of energy through successive trophic levels in an ecosystem there is a loss of energy all along the path. Studies of the transfer of energy in different food chains in a large number of ecosystems have revealed a uniform pattern of transfer of energy, which is given by the 10 percent law. According to Lindeman's 10 percent law, only 10 percent of the energy entering a particular trophic level of organisms is available for transfer to the next higher trophic level.
Example: Consider the food chain Grass → Deer → Lion. Suppose 100 J of energy is available at the grass level (producer level). According to the ten percent law, 10% of 100 J, that is 10 J of energy, will be transferred to the next trophic level of the deer (herbivore). Applying the ten percent law again, 10% of 10 J, that is 1 J of energy, will be available to the third trophic level of the lion.
Grass (100 J) — 10% → Deer (10 J) — 10% → Lion (1 J)
